prompt: pg_stat_statements shows WHERE email = $1 rather than the address that was looked up. Why?
hint: Ask what one row of that table stands for.

choices.text: The addresses are personal data, and the extension redacts them before storing
choices.why: Nothing is redacted for privacy; the literal is gone for a different reason.

choices.text: The application sent a bind parameter, so the server did not see the value
choices.why: The server saw it; the statement was normalised afterwards so that lookups by any address share a row.

choices.text: The tool counts by query, and four hundred addresses are one query
choices.why: Which is what you want when the question is what the application is doing.

choices.text: The tool records prepared statements, whose values travel separately from the text
choices.why: It sees every statement, prepared or not, and normalises the literals out of each.

prompt: One query ran 30 times at 29.7 ms each; another ran once at 114.7 ms. Which cost the server more?
hint: Multiply before you compare.

choices.text: The single one: it is the slowest per call, and the mean list ranks it first
choices.why: Slowest per call is the mean list, and it answers a different question.

choices.text: The thirty-times one: 890 ms in total against 115
choices.why: Sort by total to find what the server is spending its time on.

choices.text: Neither: both are under a second, which is below any sensible log threshold
choices.why: The log threshold is for catching the occasional slow one; it says nothing about cost.

choices.text: The single one, because a slow statement holds the fast ones waiting behind it
choices.why: A read blocks no other read; the cost is the time itself, and it adds up.

prompt: A query is fast a thousand times a day and took ten seconds once, for one customer. Which tool tells you which customer?
hint: One of the two tools keeps the literals and the other throws them away.

choices.text: The log, which writes the statement with its literals when it crosses the threshold
choices.why: log_min_duration_statement, and the ten-second run is in there with the customer's value.

choices.text: pg_stat_statements, whose row for the query carries the slowest parameter
choices.why: Its rows are normalised; the value is exactly what it does not keep.

choices.text: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query with $1, since the plan names the value
choices.why: A plan for a placeholder is a plan for nobody in particular; you need the value to run it with.

choices.text: The mean in pg_stat_statements, which ten seconds pulls up enough to see
choices.why: Ten seconds over a thousand fast runs moves the mean by ten milliseconds, and says nothing about who.

prompt: The total-time list is topped by a 0.1 ms lookup run a million times; the mean list by a 2 s report run twice a day. Support is full of complaints about waiting. Which do you work first?
hint: Ask which list a person's experience lives in.

choices.text: The lookup: it costs the server ten times more, and the server is the thing you are paid to run
choices.why: True, and it is the list to work when the machine is busy; nobody is complaining about the machine.

choices.text: Both at once, since the two lists disagree and neither can be trusted alone
choices.why: They disagree more often than not; that is why there are two, and why you pick by the question.

choices.text: Neither until the log confirms which of the two crossed the threshold
choices.why: A 2 s report is already above any sensible threshold; the log adds the literals, not the decision.

choices.text: The report: people are stuck on it, and the mean list is where a wait shows
choices.why: Two lists, two questions; the complaints answer which question is being asked today.

prompt: pg_stat_statements has to be named in ___ before the server starts, or it records nothing.
hint: A configuration setting, and it is the reason the extension cannot simply be created on a running server.

prompt: What does EXPLAIN, without ANALYZE, do with the query you give it?
hint: One verb, and it is not "run".

choices.text: Plans it and prints the plan; nothing runs, and every number is a prediction
choices.why: Every number in the output is a prediction, which is what makes ANALYZE necessary.

choices.text: Runs it and prints the plan with timings beside each step
choices.why: That is EXPLAIN ANALYZE; plain EXPLAIN executes nothing.

choices.text: Runs it without returning rows, so that it is safe to measure
choices.why: Rows are not returned under ANALYZE either, and plain EXPLAIN does not run the query at all.

choices.text: Checks the syntax and lists the tables the query names
choices.why: It goes further: it decides how each table would be read and joined.

prompt: cost=0.00..19966.00 on a Seq Scan. What are the two numbers?
hint: Neither is a time, and they are read as a start and an end.

choices.text: The minimum and the maximum time, in milliseconds
choices.why: Cost is in the planner's own unit, where one sequential page read is 1; nothing is a clock.

choices.text: The cost of reading the index and the cost of reading the table
choices.why: There is no index in a Seq Scan; the pair describes one node's start and finish.

choices.text: The cost as estimated and the cost as measured on the last run
choices.why: Both are estimates; measurements appear in a second group only under ANALYZE.

choices.text: The cost to the first row, and the cost to the last
choices.why: A scan starts at once and finishes when the table ends; an index scan pays a little to start.

prompt: What is the difference between a Filter line and an Index Cond line under a node?
hint: One of them names a condition the index answered; ask when the other one is applied.

choices.text: Filter is a condition from the WHERE clause and Index Cond one from the JOIN
choices.why: Both come from the WHERE; the difference is who answered them.

choices.text: Index Cond was answered by the index; Filter is checked on fetched rows
choices.why: A column sitting in a Filter with no Index Cond naming it is what "the index is not used" looks like.

choices.text: Index Cond is the estimated condition and Filter is the one that was measured
choices.why: Both are conditions, not numbers; the estimate and the actual sit in the parentheses.

choices.text: Filter is applied after the sort and Index Cond before the sort runs
choices.why: Neither has anything to do with a sort; both belong to the scan they sit under.

prompt: rows=11 on a Seq Scan of a million-row table. What is eleven?
hint: Not what the node reads.

choices.text: How many rows the node will read from the table before filtering
choices.why: It reads the million; eleven is what it expects to keep.

choices.text: How many pages of the table the scan is expected to touch
choices.why: Pages are in the cost and, under BUFFERS, in their own line.

choices.text: How many rows the planner expects it to pass upwards, from the statistics
choices.why: An estimate, from the statistics; comparing it with the actual is the habit the lesson builds.

choices.text: How many rows actually came back when the statement was run
choices.why: Nothing ran; the actual count appears in a second group under ANALYZE.

prompt: In an indented plan, which node does the executor work on first?
hint: Think about which way the rows flow.

choices.text: The root, which then calls each child in turn from top to bottom
choices.why: The root asks its children for rows, and cannot produce anything until they have.

choices.text: The first line printed, since the output is in execution order
choices.why: The first line printed is the root, which finishes last.

choices.text: The nodes together, in parallel, each on its own process
choices.why: Parallel plans exist and are marked with Gather; an ordinary tree runs one node's work inside another's.

choices.text: The deepest child; rows flow upwards
choices.why: Each node pulls from its children and pushes to its parent, so the bottom of the deepest branch runs first.

prompt: A one-customer join shows Seq Scan on orders with rows=1000000 under a Hash Join. What does the plan tell you that the SQL did not?
hint: Thirteen orders were wanted. Ask how many were read to find them.

choices.text: No index on the foreign key: every order was read to find thirteen
choices.why: Lesson 9's missing foreign-key index, seen from the plan's side; nothing in the SQL is wrong.

choices.text: The join condition was written the wrong way round, so the planner reversed it
choices.why: A join condition has no direction; the planner reads it either way.

choices.text: The index on customers.email is missing, so the customer was found by scanning
choices.why: It is there and it was used: the Index Scan under the Hash found the one customer.

choices.text: A hash join reads both sides in full whatever indexes exist on them
choices.why: It reads the probe side in full when nothing narrows it; with the index, the planner picks a nested loop instead.

prompt: EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM orders WHERE placed_at < DATE '2020-01-01'. What happens?
hint: The one word of caution in the section, and it is the first thing it says.

choices.text: The plan is printed and the rows stay, since EXPLAIN does not write
choices.why: Plain EXPLAIN does not; ANALYZE runs the statement, and a DELETE that runs deletes.

choices.text: The delete is simulated against a private copy of the table and discarded
choices.why: There is no copy; it is the table, and the rows are gone.

choices.text: The rows are deleted; BEGIN and ROLLBACK around it would have kept them
choices.why: ANALYZE executes whatever it is given, and a transaction is the only thing between you and the result.

choices.text: It is refused, because ANALYZE is accepted on a SELECT and not on a DELETE
choices.why: It is accepted, which is exactly the problem.

prompt: (actual time=0.002..0.003 rows=3 loops=2984). What does rows=3 mean?
hint: Every number on that line is per something.

choices.text: Three rows per loop, so about three times 2984 in total across the run
choices.why: Multiply before you believe a per-loop number; the time on that line is per loop too.

choices.text: Three rows in total, spread across the whole run of 2984 loops
choices.why: That would make 2984 loops for three rows; the count is per execution of the node.

choices.text: Three rows on the last loop, which is the one the line reports
choices.why: It is an average across the loops, not the last one.

choices.text: Three rows per millisecond, which is the node's throughput
choices.why: The time and the rows are separate measurements; neither is a rate.

prompt: Buffers: shared hit=7466 and no read= on the line. What does it say?
hint: Two words, hit and read, and one of them is missing.

choices.text: 7466 rows were returned straight from the cache without a scan
choices.why: Buffers count pages of 8 kB, not rows.

choices.text: Every page came from memory; no disk was read
choices.why: A read= entry would be the disk; its absence is the difference between slow by work and slow by disk.

choices.text: The table was read 7466 times over, once per matching row
choices.why: Once; 7466 is how many pages it has.

choices.text: 7466 pages were written back to disk at the end of the statement
choices.why: A SELECT writes nothing; hit means found in the shared buffer cache.

prompt: The same EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports 80 ms the first time and 47 ms the second, with nothing changed. What happened?
hint: Ask what the first run left behind for the second.

choices.text: The planner learnt from the first run and chose a better plan for the second
choices.why: The plan was identical; the planner keeps no memory of executions.

choices.text: The statistics were refreshed by the first run, improving the estimate
choices.why: Statistics change on ANALYZE the command, not on a query being executed.

choices.text: The second run skipped the Filter because the matching rows were known
choices.why: Every row was filtered again; nothing about the work changed, only where the pages came from.

choices.text: The first run pulled pages into the cache for the second
choices.why: Run it twice, and compare second runs or compare BUFFERS.

prompt: A report takes four minutes and you want to know why. EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE first, and why?
hint: One of them costs what the report costs.

choices.text: ANALYZE, since a plan without timings is not worth the time it takes to read
choices.why: The shape alone often names the problem, and it costs nothing to look at.

choices.text: EXPLAIN first: it is instant, and the shape names most problems
choices.why: Reach for ANALYZE when the plan looks fine and the query is not, because that gap is what only a measurement closes.

choices.text: EXPLAIN, since ANALYZE would send four minutes' worth of rows to the client
choices.why: ANALYZE returns no rows; what it costs is the four minutes of work on the server.

choices.text: ANALYZE with TIMING OFF, which drops the run time along with the clock
choices.why: TIMING OFF drops the clock overhead; the query still runs, for as long as it runs.

prompt: To keep the row counts and drop the clock's overhead: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, ___ OFF).
hint: The option that controls the per-node timing.

prompt: WHERE status = 'paid' matches 60% of orders, an index on status exists, and the plan is a Seq Scan. Is that a problem to fix?
hint: Lesson 9's argument about selectivity, with the plan in front of you.

choices.text: Yes: an index exists on the column and the planner has ignored it
choices.why: It priced both plans; following the index to most of the pages would touch them all in a worse order.

choices.text: Yes: the statistics have gone stale, or the index would have been used
choices.why: The estimate of 599 900 against 600 336 actual says the statistics are fine.

choices.text: No: text columns are not indexable, so the index there is a no-op
choices.why: Text indexes work perfectly well; the same index serves the cancelled and pending queries.

choices.text: No: sequential beats pointer-chasing to most of the pages
choices.why: A Seq Scan keeping most of the table is the right plan, and its Filter line is not a finding.

prompt: Heap Fetches: 0 on an Index Only Scan. What does it say?
hint: Heap is PostgreSQL's word for the table's own storage.

choices.text: No row was fetched from the table; the index answered everything
choices.why: The covering index of lesson 9, working as intended: the index answered everything.

choices.text: The table is empty, so there was no row to fetch
choices.why: Thirteen rows came back; the table was simply not consulted for them.

choices.text: The index is being rebuilt, so the heap was unavailable
choices.why: A rebuild would not change the plan's shape; this line counts table visits.

choices.text: The scan used no memory from the process heap
choices.why: Heap here is storage, not the process's memory.

prompt: A Bitmap Index Scan reports width=0. Why?
hint: Ask what that node hands to the node above it.

choices.text: The index has no columns of its own to return
choices.why: It has the indexed column; width is about what the node returns, and it returns no rows.

choices.text: The estimate was wrong, so the width could not be computed
choices.why: Width is an average row size, and there is no row to size.

choices.text: It returns a bitmap of pages, not rows
choices.why: One bit per page of the table, set where the index says a matching row lives.

choices.text: width is zero on each scan that goes through an index
choices.why: An Index Scan reports the width of the rows it returns; only the bitmap builder returns none.

prompt: Why does a Bitmap Heap Scan carry a Recheck Cond?
hint: Ask what a bitmap knows and what it does not.

choices.text: The rows may have changed between the index being read and the page being fetched
choices.why: Visibility is handled separately; the recheck is about precision, not time.

choices.text: A bitmap marks pages, not rows, so rows on a marked page are checked
choices.why: Which is also why exact= appears beside Heap Blocks: those pages were marked precisely.

choices.text: The planner rechecks estimates it does not trust against the real rows
choices.why: Estimates are never re-examined at run time; the recheck is a condition on rows.

choices.text: Recheck is what the Filter line is called when the index is partial
choices.why: A partial index does not change the line's name; the bitmap does.

prompt: An Index Only Scan on a table written all day shows Heap Fetches close to its row count. What is the fix?
hint: Nothing in the query changed, and lesson 9 named the structure that went stale.

choices.text: Add the fetched columns to the index with INCLUDE
choices.why: They are already in the index; the fetch is to check visibility, not to get columns.

choices.text: REINDEX, because the index has bloated with dead entries
choices.why: Bloat makes an index bigger; it does not make an index-only scan visit the table.

choices.text: Force a Bitmap Heap Scan with a planner setting
choices.why: That would fetch every row on purpose, which is the cost you are trying to remove.

choices.text: VACUUM: the visibility map is stale, so the index alone cannot prove visibility
choices.why: An index-only scan on a heavily written table stops being index-only until vacuum catches up.

prompt: Match each scan to the situation it is the answer to.
hint: Think about how many rows the query wants and where they are.

pairs.right: Most of the table is wanted
A handful of rows, in the index's order
Every column the query needs is in the index
Many rows, fetched in page order

right_distractors: The rows are wanted sorted by a column with no index
The statistics are out of date

prompt: A Nested Loop with an index scan on its inner side. When is that the right plan?
hint: One side runs once; the other runs once per row of the first.

choices.text: Both sides are large and neither fits in memory
choices.why: Then the inner side runs a large number of times; that is the hash join's case.

choices.text: A small outer side and an indexed inner side
choices.why: A few outer rows, each looked up in constant time; one customer's orders, for instance.

choices.text: Neither side has an index on the join column
choices.why: Without an index the inner side is a Seq Scan per outer row, which is the shape that is wrong.

choices.text: The join column is already sorted on both sides
choices.why: That is the merge join's case.

prompt: A Nested Loop whose inner child is a Seq Scan, with 5000 rows on the outer side. What is happening?
hint: Count how many times the inner table is read.

choices.text: The inner table is read in full 5000 times; an index is missing
choices.why: The single most common finding in a slow join, and the plan names the column.

choices.text: The inner table is hashed once and probed 5000 times from memory
choices.why: That would be a Hash Join; a Nested Loop repeats its inner child.

choices.text: Both tables are read once each and merged on the join column
choices.why: That is the Merge Join's shape, and it needs both inputs sorted.

choices.text: The outer table is read 5000 times to match each inner row
choices.why: The outer runs once; it is the inner that repeats, once per outer row.

prompt: A Hash Join reports Batches: 8. What does it mean?
hint: Ask what has to fit in memory for a hash join, and what happens when it does not.

choices.text: The join was split across eight parallel workers under a Gather node
choices.why: Workers appear under a Gather node; batches are about memory.

choices.text: Eight indexes were combined into the hash before the probe side was read
choices.why: A hash join uses no index at all; the hash is built from rows.

choices.text: The hashed side did not fit in work_mem and spilled in eight pieces
choices.why: Still a hash join, still perhaps the cheapest plan, and eight passes instead of one.

choices.text: The probe side was read eight times from the cache to match the hash
choices.why: The probe side is read once; it is the hashed side that is processed in pieces.

prompt: Which side of a join does the planner choose to hash?
hint: The hash has to fit somewhere.

choices.text: The one written first in the FROM clause
choices.why: The order in the SQL is not the order in the plan; the planner reorders freely.

choices.text: The one with an index on the join column
choices.why: A hash join does not use the index; that is the nested loop's business.

choices.text: The one with more rows, so the probe is short
choices.why: The reverse: the probe side is scanned once whatever its size, and the hashed side is the one held in memory.

choices.text: The one it estimates smaller, so that the hash fits in memory
choices.why: So that the hash fits in memory; a hash built on the wrong side points at a wrong estimate on one child.

prompt: A plan hashes a million-row table and probes it with a hundred rows. What went wrong, and where do you look?
hint: The planner hashes the side it thinks is smaller.

choices.text: work_mem: it was too small to hold the right side, so the planner hashed the other one instead
choices.why: Memory decides batches, not which side is chosen; a hundred rows fit anywhere.

choices.text: An estimate: it thought the hundred-row side was larger; compare rows= on both children
choices.why: The plan did the right thing for its numbers; one of the numbers is off by orders of magnitude.

choices.text: The join order in the SQL, which the planner follows when both sides are indexed
choices.why: The planner ignores the written order; nothing in the SQL decides which side is hashed.

choices.text: The index on the hundred-row side, which forced it to become the probe
choices.why: Indexes play no part in a hash join's choice of sides.

prompt: loops=3 on a node under a Gather with Workers Launched: 2. What is three?
hint: Count the processes.

choices.text: The node ran three times because its estimate was wrong each time
choices.why: Loops under a Gather are processes, not retries.

choices.text: Three retries after the two workers failed and the leader took over
choices.why: A failed worker fails the query; nothing is retried.

choices.text: The leader and two workers, each reporting its own share of the rows
choices.why: A node under a Gather reports per worker, and there are three processes doing the work.

choices.text: Three batches of the hash, one per process
choices.why: Batches have their own line; loops count executions of the node.

prompt: WHERE date(placed_at) = DATE '2025-03-01' estimated 5000 rows and returned 1834. Why 5000?
hint: Ask what the planner has statistics about, and what it does not.

choices.text: The statistics said 5000 orders were placed that day, and they were out of date
choices.why: There are no statistics for that day or any other, because there are none for date(placed_at).

choices.text: There are no statistics for a function's result, so a default fraction was used
choices.why: Half a percent of a million, whatever the table holds; the rewrite as a range fixes it.

choices.text: 5000 is the planner's estimate for any equality condition on a large table
choices.why: An equality on a bare column is estimated from that column's distribution; this one had none.

choices.text: The index on placed_at reported 5000 entries for that date, before it was refused
choices.why: No index was consulted; a function around the column rules it out, and the plan is a Seq Scan.

prompt: A table that has never been analysed: after loading 200 000 rows, EXPLAIN says rows=754 for a condition that matches a quarter of them. What fixes the estimate?
hint: One statement, and the planner goes from guessing to knowing.

choices.text: ANALYZE the table
choices.why: Statistics are collected on demand or by autovacuum, and neither had run since the load.

choices.text: VACUUM FULL, to rebuild the statistics with the table
choices.why: VACUUM FULL rewrites the table; it is ANALYZE that collects statistics, and the FULL costs a lock for nothing here.

choices.text: CREATE INDEX on the filtered column
choices.why: An index changes how rows are found, not how many the planner expects.

choices.text: Wait: the estimate corrects itself on the next query
choices.why: A query executing changes no statistics; autovacuum will get to it eventually, and the bad plans live in the gap.

prompt: Reading the estimates on a deep plan, where do you start and where do you stop?
hint: Every node above a mistake inherits it.

choices.text: From the root, since the total time is there
choices.why: The root's estimate is the product of every mistake below it; it cannot say where the first one was.

choices.text: At the join, since a scan's estimate comes straight from the statistics
choices.why: Scans are where two of the commonest misestimates live: a function around the column, and a table never analysed.

choices.text: At the node with the largest actual time, which is the one costing the most
choices.why: The slowest node is often a correct plan for a wrong estimate made further down.

choices.text: From the bottom, stopping at the first node where the two numbers disagree by a large factor
choices.why: A factor of two is noise; a factor of a hundred is the finding, and everything above it inherited it.

prompt: WHERE city = 'Manaus' AND state = 'AM' is estimated far too low, though each column alone is estimated well. Why, and what fixes it?
hint: The planner has an assumption about two conditions, and these two break it.

choices.text: The two columns need a composite index before the planner will estimate them together
choices.why: An index changes how rows are found; the estimate would be just as wrong with one.

choices.text: The string comparison is case-sensitive and misses the rows in other spellings
choices.why: Nothing is missed; the rows come back, and only the prediction of how many is wrong.

choices.text: The planner multiplies the two selectivities; CREATE STATISTICS on the pair
choices.why: After that it has a joint distribution, and an address in Manaus is no longer allowed to be in any state.

choices.text: ANALYZE, which collects the joint distribution of each column pair by default
choices.why: ANALYZE collects per-column statistics; the pair has to be declared before it will look at both together.

prompt: A query is fast in psql with a literal and slow from the application, which sends a placeholder. First suspect?
hint: Ask which value the application's plan was made for.

choices.text: A generic plan built for the average value
choices.why: A plan for $1 is a plan for the average, and the average status is paid, at sixty percent; wrong for a rare value.

choices.text: The application's connection is slower than psql's, so the rows take longer
choices.why: The connection carries the rows; a slow plan is slow on any connection.

choices.text: The driver strips the index hint that psql keeps in the statement
choices.why: PostgreSQL has no index hints to strip; the plan is chosen from statistics either way.

choices.text: psql caches the result of the query and the application does not
choices.why: Neither caches results; the cache that exists holds pages, and both benefit from it alike.

prompt: PostgreSQL 10 and later can be told that two columns are related, with CREATE ___.
hint: The object that gives the planner a joint distribution.

prompt: Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 26kB, on a million rows with LIMIT 10. How did a million rows sort in 26 kB?
hint: The sort knew something from the node above it.

choices.text: The rows were already nearly in order, so little had to move
choices.why: Order does not change the memory a full sort needs; the trick is what was kept.

choices.text: The sort ran on disk, and 26 kB is the index it kept in memory
choices.why: Disk would say external merge and name the size; this one stayed in memory.

choices.text: It kept a heap of ten and dropped the rest as it read
choices.why: The Limit above it said only ten would ever be wanted, and that is why LIMIT is cheap.

choices.text: Just ten rows were read from the table, so ten were sorted
choices.why: The Seq Scan below it returned a million; the sort is what threw them away.

prompt: Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 38576kB. Which word matters, and what does it say?
hint: One word in that line is the finding.

choices.text: merge: the sort was done by a Merge Join rather than a Sort node
choices.why: No join is involved; merge describes how the sorted runs were combined.

choices.text: Disk: the rows exceeded work_mem and were sorted in runs on disk
choices.why: A sort that spills is the commonest reason a query fine at ten thousand rows is slow at a million.

choices.text: external: the sort was handed to the operating system's own sort
choices.why: External means outside memory; the database did the sorting, on its own temporary files.

choices.text: 38576kB: the size of the result that was sent back to the client
choices.why: It is the temporary space the sort used, and ANALYZE sends no result at all.

prompt: Three fixes for a sort that spills: fewer rows, an index to read from, more work_mem. Why is work_mem the last to try?
hint: Ask who else gets the same allowance.

choices.text: Changing it needs a restart of the server, which is a maintenance window
choices.why: It can be set per session and per role; the trouble is not how it is changed.

choices.text: It applies to hash joins and not to sorts, so the sort would spill anyway
choices.why: It applies to both, which makes the multiplication worse rather than better.

choices.text: A bigger work_mem makes the planner prefer sequential scans over indexes
choices.why: It changes what fits in memory; it does not turn index scans into sequential ones.

choices.text: It is granted per sort in every connection, and multiplies under load
choices.why: A per-sort allowance, multiplied by every sort running at once, and a number that fixes one report exhausts the server.

prompt: HashAggregate or GroupAggregate: when does the second one appear?
hint: One of them needs its input in a particular order.

choices.text: When the input is already sorted, or there are too many groups to hash
choices.why: It counts each run as it passes; neither is better, and the line beside the node says whether it fit.

choices.text: When the GROUP BY names more than one column and the groups nest
choices.why: Either aggregate handles any number of grouping columns.

choices.text: When a HAVING clause is present, since a hash has no way to filter groups
choices.why: HAVING filters groups after either aggregate has made them.

choices.text: When the query also has an ORDER BY on the grouping column
choices.why: The city report has an ORDER BY and hashed anyway, sorting the ten groups afterwards.

prompt: A Sort node appears in a plan whose query has no ORDER BY. Which of these is NOT a possible reason?
hint: Three nodes need their input ordered, and one does not.

choices.text: A Merge Join needing both inputs ordered
choices.why: A real reason: both sides have to be sorted on the join column.

choices.text: A HashAggregate needing its input sorted before it groups
choices.why: A hash aggregate needs no order at all; that is what the hash is for.

choices.text: A GroupAggregate needing its groups adjacent
choices.why: A real reason: it counts runs, so equal keys must sit together.

choices.text: A DISTINCT done by sorting the rows
choices.why: A real reason: sort, then drop each row equal to the one before it.

prompt: The plan shows Seq Scan with Filter: (lower(email) = …), and a unique index on email exists. What do you try first?
hint: The first item on the list is not an index.

choices.text: Add a second index on email, since the first one is being ignored
choices.why: The second would be ignored for the same reason: the query asks about lower(email), and neither holds that.

choices.text: Rewrite the query, or index the expression, so the two name the same thing
choices.why: So that the query and the index name the same thing; nothing here needed a new index of the ordinary kind.

choices.text: Raise work_mem so that the filter can run in memory
choices.why: A filter does not use work_mem; it checks each row as it passes, and the rows are the cost.

choices.text: Run ANALYZE so that the planner notices the index exists
choices.why: The planner sees the index; it cannot use it for an expression the index does not hold.

prompt: OFFSET 500000 LIMIT 20 read 500 020 rows through the index; WHERE id > 500000 LIMIT 20 read twenty. Why the difference?
hint: Ask where in the index each version is able to start.

choices.text: Keyset paging uses a smaller index, which fits in the cache
choices.why: Both used the same primary key index; the difference is where they began in it.

choices.text: OFFSET disables the index and forces a sequential scan of the table
choices.why: The plan shows an Index Scan for both; OFFSET walks the index and throws rows away.

choices.text: The keyset version starts in the index at the right place
choices.why: OFFSET has to walk past everything it skips; keyset paging costs the same on page one and page twenty-five thousand.

choices.text: The keyset version returns fewer columns, so fewer pages are read
choices.why: Both are SELECT *; the columns are identical.

prompt: SELECT * became SELECT customer_id, and the scan turned index-only. What is the general lesson?
hint: Lesson 4's argument, with a plan attached.

choices.text: SELECT * is slower because the star has to be expanded at run time
choices.why: Expansion is at planning time and costs nothing; the pages fetched are the cost.

choices.text: Single-column queries are planned by a different, simpler algorithm
choices.why: Same planner, same algorithm; the index simply covered what was asked.

choices.text: customer_id is cached and the other columns of the row are not
choices.why: Caching is by page, not by column; the other columns live in the table pages that were not read.

choices.text: Unneeded columns cost pages read, and the plan shows it
choices.why: Three columns needed and twenty asked for is seventeen columns' worth of row fetches.

prompt: enable_seqscan = off fixed the slow query in your session. Do you put it in postgresql.conf?
hint: Ask what the setting does to every other query on the server.

choices.text: No: the planner would misprice every query on the server
choices.why: Including the ones that were fine; the settings exist for seeing an alternative plan in a session, never for shipping one.

choices.text: Yes, since the plan is now the correct one for this query
choices.why: It is the correct plan for this query and a lie told to the planner about every other.

choices.text: Yes, with enable_indexscan = on beside it so the rest stays as it is
choices.why: Index scans are already on; the harm is in what was switched off.

choices.text: No: the setting has no effect outside a psql session
choices.why: It affects every session that has it, which in the configuration file is all of them.

prompt: A report runs once a month and would be fast with a new index on a table taking a million inserts a day. What do you do?
hint: Lesson 9's tax, and pg_stat_statements says how often the query runs.

choices.text: Add the index: a slow report is a slow report, and the writes will cope
choices.why: It would be maintained on a million writes a day to save one query a month.

choices.text: Add it CONCURRENTLY, which makes it free to build and cheap to maintain
choices.why: CONCURRENTLY is about building without a lock; maintenance costs the same afterwards.

choices.text: Leave the table alone; a materialised view or a replica is the place
choices.why: Changing the shape of the work, which is the last item on the list for the queries that do a lot correctly.

choices.text: Add it before each run and drop it afterwards, so the writes do not pay
choices.why: Building it reads the whole table, which is the report's own cost again, with a lock or two passes on top.

prompt: Put the five things to change in the order the lesson says to try them.
hint: The cheap ones come first because they make the expensive ones unnecessary.
items: Rewrite the query so the index that exists can apply
Add the index the plan is asking for, concurrently
Ask for fewer columns and fewer rows
Fix the estimate: ANALYZE, or extended statistics
Change the shape of the work: a materialised view or a replica
trap: The common swap is adding an index before checking whether the query refuses one it already has — a permanent cost on writes to fix what a rewrite would have fixed for nothing.

prompt: MySQL's EXPLAIN shows type: ALL on a row. What is it?
hint: The column says how the table is accessed.

choices.text: A full table scan, which is the Seq Scan of this lesson
choices.why: The Seq Scan of this lesson; on any row but the first it is the missing-index shape, the whole table read once per outer row.

choices.text: The table is accessed through each of its indexes
choices.why: The index used is in the key column; ALL means none was.

choices.text: The join keeps the whole table's rows
choices.why: type describes access, not what the join returns.

choices.text: The row count is unknown
choices.why: rows is its own column; ALL is about how, not how many.

prompt: Using filesort appears in MySQL's Extra column. What does it mean?
hint: The line people misread, and the word file is the reason.

choices.text: The sort was written to a temporary file on disk
choices.why: It may have stayed in memory; the name is older than the behaviour.

choices.text: The rows were sorted by the file system rather than the server
choices.why: The server sorts; the file system stores.

choices.text: The query sorts by a column that is not in the SELECT list
choices.why: Sorting by an unselected column is allowed and says nothing about filesort.

choices.text: A sort happened because no index supplied the order
choices.why: In memory or not: MySQL's spelling of a Sort node with no index under it, and the fix is the same.

prompt: In what order does MySQL's EXPLAIN list its rows?
hint: One row per table, and the order says something about how the join runs.

choices.text: Alphabetically by table name, which makes the rows easy to find
choices.why: The order carries meaning; alphabetical would carry none.

choices.text: The order the tables appear in the FROM clause, as written
choices.why: The planner reorders joins freely, and the output shows what it chose.

choices.text: The join order, driving table first
choices.why: Top to bottom, the way a nested loop runs; type: ALL below the first row is the missing index.

choices.text: Largest table first, since that is the one the planner reads first
choices.why: Size is one input to the choice; the output is the order chosen.

prompt: SQLite's EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN prints SCAN orders. What does it mean?
hint: Two words make up its whole vocabulary.

choices.text: The bytecode for reading the orders table
choices.why: Bytecode is what plain EXPLAIN prints, and it is not what anybody wants.

choices.text: A full read of the table, with no index used
choices.why: SEARCH … USING INDEX would be the index lookup; that pair is the vocabulary, and the fix is in it.

choices.text: The table is being analysed for statistics
choices.why: ANALYZE is a separate command in SQLite, and it prints nothing like this.

choices.text: An index on orders is being scanned in full
choices.why: An index would be named after USING INDEX; SCAN alone is the table.

prompt: A SQLite database grew tenfold over a year and its plans are now bad. Why, unlike PostgreSQL, and what do you do?
hint: Ask who collects the statistics in each engine.

choices.text: SQLite keeps no planner statistics of any kind, so the fix is to rebuild the indexes
choices.why: It has them; they come from ANALYZE, and rebuilding an index collects none.

choices.text: SQLite plans from the size of the file, so VACUUM the file down
choices.why: VACUUM compacts the file; the planner's numbers come from ANALYZE.

choices.text: SQLite lacks EXPLAIN ANALYZE, so its plans are not improvable once they go bad
choices.why: Measurement is what SQLite lacks; the statistics that decide a plan are one command away.

choices.text: SQLite has no autovacuum to collect statistics; run ANALYZE yourself
choices.why: A database that grew a lot since it was last analysed is planning on old numbers until somebody runs the command.
